item.title: Nonlinear Reduced-Bias Extreme Value Index Estimators: A Comparative Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.34308v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The estimation of the extreme value index (EVI) plays a central role in extreme value theory (EVT), particularly in the statistical modelling of heavy-tailed phenomena. Classical semi-parametric estimators of the EVI are known to suffer from substantial bias, especially for moderate sample sizes and for common choices of the number of upper order statistics. In recent years, several reduced-bias (RB) methodologies have been proposed in order to improve finite-sample performance while preserving asymptotic efficiency. In this paper, we present new classes of nonlinear RB EVI-estimators based on power mean-type and Lehmer mean-type functionals of upper log-excesses. Under a unified higher-order framework, asymptotic representations are derived and bias and variance properties are compared relative to other RB EVI classes introduced in the literature. An asymptotic comparison at optimal levels is conducted to identify regions of the space parameter where the proposed estimators are more efficient. A comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation study assesses the finite sample behaviour of the new estimators for several heavy tailed models. The results show that nonlinear reduced-bias estimators can provide improvements in bias and root mean squared error, although their relative performance depends on the underlying distribution and the choice of the tuning parameter. An application to hydrological data illustrates their practical use and the importance of threshold selection in EVI estimation.
item.dc:creator: L\'igia Henriques-Rodrigues, Frederico Caeiro, M. Ivette Gomes

item.title: A functional central limit theorem for particle systems under polynomial growth conditions, with applications to statistics
item.description: arXiv:2610.34347v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish a functional central limit theorem (CLT) for fluctuations of time-integrated functionals of empirical measures arising from interacting McKean--Vlasov particle systems. Our framework allows for coefficients with unbounded spatial growth and dependence on arbitrarily high-order moments of the measure variable, extending the scope of the existing fluctuation theory. The proof uses a novel approach combining linear functional differentiation with new well-posedness results and estimates for perturbed backward parabolic equations in polynomially weighted Schauder spaces, yielding a martingale-type representation of the fluctuations with an asymptotically negligible remainder. The limiting process is shown to be centred Gaussian with an explicit covariance structure. As a statistical application, we derive the asymptotic theory underlying hypothesis tests for both the temporal constancy of population characteristics and parametric restrictions on the drift coefficient.
item.dc:creator: Mark Podolskij, Fabrice Wunderlich

item.title: Inference for Causal Path-Specific Effects in Longitudinal Studies with Repeated Treatments and Multiple Mediators
item.description: arXiv:2610.34349v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In longitudinal studies, repeated treatments may be followed by different sequences of mediators and time-varying covariates. We develop semiparametric inference for path-specific effects in this setting, allowing the number, type, and ordering of intermediate variables to vary across treatment occasions. Under consistency, positivity, edge consistency, and the cross-world restrictions of a nonparametric structural equation model with independent errors, path-specific means are identified by the edge g-formula. We derive two parameterizations of the efficient influence function of the identifying functional. The first follows the observed-data factorization and uses conditional intermediate-variable densities. The second uses sequential regressions to replace the corresponding integrations and Bayes' rule to express density ratios through treatment-history regressions, thereby avoiding direct estimation of intermediate-variable densities. Each yields a one-step estimator that permits flexible nuisance estimation. We establish product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and semiparametric efficiency. The density-based estimator has blockwise multiple robustness, generalizing triply robust estimation, while the regression-based estimator has sequential multiple robustness. We further develop a sensitivity analysis for selected violations of cross-world independence assumptions used to identify these effects. Simulations examine finite-sample performance and robustness to model misspecifications. An application to the Framingham Heart Study examines sustained-smoking effects on systolic blood pressure along pathways through repeated body mass index measurements. The proposed methods are implemented in the R package flexPaths on Gihub at xxou/flexPaths.
item.dc:creator: Xiaxian Ou, Xinwei He, Razieh Nabi

item.title: Intrinsic Gradient Barriers in Pushforward Deep Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.34484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Broad classes of deep generative models (DGMs) operate by learning to map a simple source distribution, such as a standard Gaussian, to a complex high-dimensional target distribution. Despite their success, DGMs often empirically struggle to accurately represent distributions with heavy tails or well-separated modes. In this work, we show that these difficulties reflect intrinsic properties of the underlying transport problem rather than particular neural network architectures or training procedures. We establish quantitative lower bounds on the gradients and Jacobians of pushforward mappings that transport log-concave source distributions to such targets. For heavy-tailed target distributions, the required gradient magnitude grows as the target develops increasingly large moments. For multimodal target distributions, the low-probability regions between well-separated modes similarly force large gradients in the transport map. We discuss how such large derivatives relate to trade-offs between expressivity and numerical stability. Our results hold under substantially weaker regularity conditions than previous analyses and remain stable under perturbations of the target distribution. Finally, we show that these obstructions can be mitigated when the goal is approximation of a given density rather than generative modeling. Specifically, we propose simple classes of bijective reparametrizations that can alleviate the difficult geometric structure and reduce the gradient burden placed on the learned generative map. Numerical experiments support our theoretical analysis.
item.dc:creator: Edric Tam, Qingyang Liu, Barbara Engelhardt, Ray Bai

item.title: The German Tank Problem & Navigating by Scent
item.description: arXiv:2610.34583v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A robot searching for the source of an odor must eventually answer a deceptively hard question: have I arrived? Near the source, concentration gradients flatten, turbulence makes the signal intermittent, and a small robot often lacks the positional accuracy to map the plume. Here, we describe a lightweight remedy inspired by a World War II statistics conundrum: the German tank problem. To approximate enemy armament production, Allied analysts developed an estimator based on serial numbers from captured tanks. Analogously, we use the same procedure over sampled chemical sensor readings from a robot to create estimates for the peak concentration of an odor plume, and therefore the odor's source. Treating each sensor reading as an observation, our unbiased estimator needs only a running maximum and a sample counter. An exact confidence bound turns both numbers into a principled rule that the robot or UAV can use to determine whether to keep searching for the plume source or land. We derive the estimator and its bound, demonstrate its sample efficiency, and examine its robustness even when its assumptions fail. Finally, we summarize the estimator's role as the termination criterion for olfactory navigation.
item.dc:creator: Kordel Kade France

item.title: A new categorical correlation measure
item.description: arXiv:2610.34932v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Feature screening in high-dimensional classification is an important problem in statistical learning, particularly in genomics, imaging, and other scientific fields, especially when the number of predictors exceeds the sample size. Zhong et al. (2024) present a semi-distance covariance (SDCov) as a dependence measure between a categorical random variable and a multivariate continuous random vector, presenting it as a promising tool for group-wise feature screening. However, SDCov is defined using the Euclidean norm, and its performance may be affected when the data is derived from heavy-tailed distributions or when outlier observations are present, which is a common phenomenon in high-dimensional data. This study proposes a modification of SDCov by replacing the $L_2$ norm with an $L_1$ norm. This adjustment results in a dependency measure between a categorical variable and a multivariate continuous variable that maintains the independence-characterization property of the original definition. Additionally, it serves as a robust and interpretable measure, particularly in the presence of outliers in the data. We establish the fundamental theoretical properties of the proposed measure and introduce a U-statistics-based estimator along with JEL-based inference for the measure. Additionally, we have introduced a test for independence based on the proposed measure. An extensive Monte Carlo simulation is performed to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed measure in comparison to existing measures in the literature. The proposed measure is applied in feature screening, as illustrated with the ADNI Alzheimer's disease dataset and the Iris dataset. The data analysis shows the proposed measure's effectiveness in identifying variables that facilitate strong class separation of the respective response variables.
item.dc:creator: Saparya Suresh, Sudheesh K. Kattumannil, Sujit Ghosh

item.title: Comparing and measuring intermediate tail dependence
item.description: arXiv:2610.35325v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The tail dependence function $\Lambda$ of a bivariate copula, and the tail dependence order based on it, cannot distinguish between copulas whose tail dependence coefficient vanishes; for all of them $\Lambda\equiv 0$. Such copulas, among them the Gaussian copulas with correlation $\rho<1$ and the lower tails of all extreme-value copulas other than the comonotonicity copula, are nevertheless ordered by the much finer information contained in their tail expansion $C(u w)\sim u^{\kappa}\ell(u)\,b(w)$, where $\kappa$ is the tail order, $\ell$ is slowly varying and $b$ is the tail order function of Hua and Joe. We introduce an asymptotic tail order $\preceq$ that refines the tail dependence order and show that it is lexicographic in the three quantities $\kappa$, $\ell$ and $b$. As a consequence, every real-valued measure that is monotone with respect to $\preceq$ is constant on all but countably many tail-order classes; meaningful measures of intermediate tail dependence must therefore be defined level-wise, and we construct such measures. Finally we determine where the fine structure resides: if the joint tail is ray-regular on the exponential scale, then $b$ is determined by the tail order and the one-sided derivatives at $\omega=1/2$ of the angular dependence function of Wadsworth and Tawn; it is a (possibly broken) product of powers. If the joint tail is log-concave on the exponential scale, $b$ is squeezed between two such products.
item.dc:creator: Karl Friedrich Siburg

item.title: Distribution-free predictive inference with instrumental variables
item.description: arXiv:2610.35605v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the problem of predictive inference with outcomes missing not at random, when instrumental variables are available. While conformal prediction and weighted conformal prediction provide valid distribution-free inference when outcomes are missing completely at random and missing at random, respectively, inference is generally not possible without additional assumptions when outcomes are missing not at random. In this work, we consider a setting where we remain within the distribution-free framework but instead have access to an instrumental variable (IV). We explore the theoretical possibility of IV predictive inference and establish that it is characterized by a parameter that we refer to as the identification index. We derive an impossibility result for the case where the identification index is not sufficiently large, showing that any distribution-free approach fails to provide informative inference in this case. For the case where the identification index is sufficiently large, we introduce a practical method that achieves informative predictive inference. Our method leverages modern semiparametric efficiency theory which involves deriving the efficient influence function of the identifying functional for sharp IV bounds of the quantiles of the missing outcome, delivering a double robustness property in the coverage guarantee of the proposed framework for IV-based predictive inference. We illustrate the theoretical results and the performance of the proposed procedure through simulations and two real-data applications---FES wages and NHANES III self-reported heights.
item.dc:creator: Yonghoon Lee, Edgar Dobriban, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen

item.title: Provably Efficient Q-learning for Robust Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.35656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms based on Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps. To address this issue, distributionally robust RL algorithms based on robust MDPs (RMDPs) have been proposed, for ensuring that agents can perform reliably to unpredictable conditions in real-world environments. Despite of the rich literature, \revision{an efficient model-free method is still lacking} for robust RL, particularly for Markovian data, which is more relevant in practical applications. In this work, we take a step towards settling this problem by proposing a sample efficient (asynchronous Q-learning) algorithm for robust RL. In particular, consider a $\gamma$-discounted infinite-horizon RMDP with state space $\mathcal{S}$ and action space $\mathcal{A}$, where the uncertainty set is specified by the total variation (TV) distance with uncertainty level $\sigma$. Assuming access to a single trajectory of Markovian samples induced by a behavior policy and the nominal transition kernel, the sample complexity of the proposed Q-learning algorithm --- to achieve an entrywise $\varepsilon$-approximation of the optimal Q-function --- is bounded by $$ \frac{1}{\mu_{\mathsf{min}}\varepsilon^2(1-\gamma)^3\max\{1-\gamma,\sigma\}} + \frac{t_{\mathsf{mix}}}{\mu_{\mathsf{min}}(1-\gamma)} $$ up to logarithmic factors. Here, $t_{\mathsf{mix}}$ and $\mu_{\mathsf{min}}$ denote the mixing time and the minimum state-action occupancy probability of the sample trajectory, respectively. This result is nearly minimax optimal, with an additional factor of $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$. Moreover, it achieves a significant improvement over existing bounds.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Jiao, Gen Li

item.title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
item.description: arXiv:2610.35821v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Statistical procedures often control expected loss at a prescribed level while leaving part of their risk budget unused. Building on the e-value representation of risk-controlled decisions and the e-closure principle for multiple testing, we formulate recertification, a general paradigm for improving procedures by exploiting computable slack in their validity certificates. A valid procedure's losses normalized by their risk budgets form a state-indexed e-value collection; conversely, decisions whose normalized losses are bounded by this collection inherit its risk guarantees. Recertification uses distributional structure to quantify slack, enlarge the certifying e-values while preserving validity, and construct less conservative decisions. We develop two applications. For conformal risk control (CRC) with a known loss family, recertification redistributes unused risk budget among the held-out points of each hypothetical augmented sample. The resulting controller is valid under every finite exchangeable law and no more conservative than CRC on any calibration sample. For convex losses on an interval of actions, repeated recertification converges geometrically to an admissible controller. For false discovery rate control with arbitrarily dependent e-values, recertification exploits unused conditional budgets in randomized e-BH. It yields a closed-form randomized procedure whose rejection set contains that of randomized e-BH for every realization of the shared randomization and whose expected number of rejections is maximal subject to the same conditional budget constraints. Recertifying with the larger e-collection of closed e-BH gives a second closed-form procedure whose rejection set contains that of the first. Experiments on CIFAR-100 hierarchical classification and multiple testing simulations demonstrate improved budget utilization, informativeness and power over the baselines.
item.dc:creator: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Compatibility-based Bayesian inference: asymptotic limits, variational principles, and Wasserstein geometry
item.description: arXiv:2105.01962v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) replaces intractable likelihood evaluations with comparisons between observed and simulated data. We formulate discrepancy-based inference through nonnegative compatibility weights. Prior-integrated convergence of rescaled weights gives total variation convergence as the tolerance vanishes. For a fixed positive tolerance and increasing sample size, we give a general representation-based formulation of the conditional-prior limit known from ABC and coarsened Bayesian inference, and establish convergence in expected total variation under stabilization in probability and a prior-null boundary condition. We also derive acceptance-persistence bounds under partial stabilization. The Gibbs variational identity yields convergence of minimum values and stability of approximate minimizers; the fixed-tolerance limit is characterized separately by constrained relative-entropy minimization. For additional penalty-based functionals of the limiting Wasserstein discrepancy, we prove an exact reduction to distributions over model laws and, under a geodesic assumption, a representation by distances from a Wasserstein ball. These penalty-based updates are distinguished from the original fixed-tolerance ABC limit and illustrated through a Gaussian comparison.
item.dc:creator: Marco Tarsia, Antonietta Mira, Daniele Cassani

item.title: A theory of stratification learning
item.description: arXiv:2405.20066v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given i.i.d. sample from a stratified mixture of immersed manifolds of different dimensions, we study the minimax estimation of the underlying stratified structure. We provide a constructive algorithm allowing to estimate each mixture component at its optimal dimension-specific rate adaptively. The method is based on an ascending hierarchical co-detection of points belonging to different layers, which also identifies the number of layers and their dimensions, assigns each data point to a layer accurately, and estimates tangent spaces optimally. These results hold regardless of any ambient assumption on the manifolds or on their intersection configurations. They open the way to a broad clustering framework, where each mixture component models a cluster emanating from a specific nonlinear correlation phenomenon.
item.dc:creator: Eddie Aamari, Cl\'ement Berenfeld

item.title: Simultaneous analysis of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation and mean-field inference
item.description: arXiv:2501.02624v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approximate Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (ALO-CV) is a method that has been proposed to estimate the generalization error of a regularized estimator in the high-dimensional regime where dimension and sample size are of the same order, the so-called ``proportional regime''. A new analysis is developed to derive the consistency of ALO-CV for non-differentiable regularizers under Gaussian covariates and strong convexity. Using a conditioning argument, the difference between the ALO-CV weights and their counterparts in mean-field inference is shown to be small. Combined with upper bounds between the mean-field inference estimate and the leave-one-out quantity, this provides a proof that ALO-CV approximates the leave-one-out quantity up to negligible error terms. Linear models with square loss, robust linear regression and single-index models are explicitly treated.
item.dc:creator: Pierre C Bellec

item.title: Bayesian Predictive Inference Beyond Martingales
item.description: arXiv:2507.21874v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There is growing interest in the so-called Bayesian Predictive Inference approach, which enables Bayesian inference without specifying a likelihood function or prior distribution and without resorting to MCMC methods. Instead, only a sequence of predictive distributions for the observations is required, and inference on the unknown estimand can be performed, cheaply in parallel, using bootstrap-type schemes. Understanding which classes of predictive distributions can be used within this framework, is still a key open question. We relax commonly used probabilistic assumptions on the observations, namely exchangeability and conditionally identical distribution, and on their predictive distributions, which are measure-valued martingales, by introducing the new class of Almost Conditionally Identically Distributed (a.c.i.d.) random variables. This class assumes that the predictive distributions are measure-valued almost supermartingales, and is parametrized by a sequence of parameters $(\xi_{n})_{n\geq 0}$, which regulate the decay of conditional dependence among future observations. Under mild summability assumptions on $(\xi_{n})_{n\geq 0}$, the resulting sequence of observations is shown to be asymptotically exchangeable, hence amenable to Bayesian Predictive Inference techniques. A.c.i.d. random variables arise naturally in recursive algorithms, and include classic approaches in Statistics and Learning Theory, such as kernel estimators, and more novel ones, such as the parametric Bayesian bootstrap.
item.dc:creator: Marco Battiston, Lorenzo Cappello

item.title: Geometric Identification and Consistent Estimation of Source Apportionment with Application to Greenland Summit Aerosols
item.description: arXiv:2510.03616v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Over the last four decades, the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the rest of the planet, with anthropogenic aerosols among the major forcings. Greenland Summit Station has collected size-resolved particulate matter year-round since 2003, yet these records remain underutilized. Attributing multipollutant measurements to their sources (source apportionment) can be cast as a non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) problem. Because NMF is non-unique, source apportionment imposes often unverifiable constraints such as structural sparsity or rotations tuned using prior scientific knowledge, which is scarce for remote regions like the Arctic. Geometric NMF approaches offer a more data-driven route to identification, but many suffer from scaling ambiguity, assume exact separability, and lack a statistical framework for consistent estimation. We address these limitations by formally establishing statistical identifiability of the source attribution matrix under a stochastic framework that replaces hard separability with soft probabilistic relaxations. We then present a scalable geometric algorithm to estimate this matrix and prove its consistency, to our knowledge the first such result requiring no exact sparsity, no parametric distributional assumptions, and accommodating spatio-temporal dependence. Analyzing the 2003--2016 Summit record with our framework and HYSPLIT trajectories, we characterize long-range transport of anthropogenic and natural species into the Arctic.
item.dc:creator: Bora Jin, Nicholas J. Spada, Jessie Creamean, Matthew Shupe, Abhirup Datta

item.title: Wasserstein-Cram\'er-Rao Theory of Unbiased Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2511.07414v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The quantity of interest in the classical Cram\'er-Rao theory of unbiased estimation (e.g., the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound, its exact attainment for exponential families, and asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood estimation) is the variance, which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an independently-sampled data set from the same distribution. In this paper we are interested in a quantity which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an infinitesimal additive perturbation of the original data set; we refer to this as the "sensitivity" of an estimator. The resulting theory of sensitivity is based on the Wasserstein geometry in the same way that the classical theory of variance is based on the Fisher-Rao (equivalently, Hellinger) geometry, and this insight allows us to determine a collection of results which are analogous to the classical case: a Wasserstein-Cram\'er-Rao lower bound for the sensitivity of any unbiased estimator, a characterization of models in which there exist unbiased estimators achieving the lower bound exactly, and various results on the asymptotic achievement of the lower bound. More precisely, we show that Wasserstein projection estimators (and one-step approximations thereof) are asymptotically sensitivity-efficient under suitable assumptions, and that there exist Hodges-type estimators which exhibit super-sensitivity-efficiency. We use these results to treat many statistical examples, sometimes revealing new optimality properties for existing estimators and other times revealing entirely new estimators.
item.dc:creator: Nicol\'as Garc\'ia Trillos, Adam Quinn Jaffe, Bodhisattva Sen

item.title: New Empirical Process Tools and Their Applications to Robust Deep ReLU Networks and Phase Transitions for Nonparametric Regression
item.description: arXiv:2511.15841v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces new empirical process tools for analyzing a broad class of statistical learning models under heavy-tailed noise and complex function classes. Our primary contribution is the derivation of two Dudley-type maximal inequalities for expected empirical processes that remove restrictive assumptions such as light tails and uniform boundedness of the function class. These inequalities enlarge the scope of empirical process theory available for statistical learning and nonparametric estimation. Exploiting the new bounds, we establish robustness guarantees for deep ReLU network estimators in Huber and quantile regression. In particular, we prove a unified non-asymptotic sub-Gaussian concentration bound that remains valid even under infinite-variance noise and provide a comprehensive analysis of non-asymptotic robustness for deep Huber estimators across all noise regimes. For deep quantile regression, we provide the first non-asymptotic sub-Gaussian bounds without requiring moment assumptions. As an additional application, our framework yields estimation error bounds for nonparametric least-squares estimators that simultaneously accommodate infinite-variance noise, non-Donsker function classes, and approximation error. Moreover, unlike prior approaches based on specialized multiplier processes, our framework extends to broader empirical risk minimization problems, including the nonparametric generalized linear models and the ``set-structured'' models.
item.dc:creator: Yizhe Ding, Runze Li, Lingzhou Xue

item.title: Minimaxity and Admissibility of Bayesian Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2604.04673v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a natural probabilistic formulation for inference in deep learning models. Despite their popularity, their optimality has received limited attention through the lens of statistical decision theory. In this paper, we study decision rules induced by deep, fully connected feedforward ReLU BNNs in the normal location model under quadratic loss. We show that, for fixed prior scales, the induced Bayes decision rule is not minimax. We then propose a hyperprior on the effective output variance of the BNN prior that yields a superharmonic square-root marginal density, establishing that the resulting decision rule is simultaneously admissible and minimax. We further extend these results from the quadratic loss setting to the predictive density estimation problem with Kullback--Leibler loss. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings numerically through simulation.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Andrew Coulson, Martin T. Wells

item.title: Minimax Robust Designs for M-Estimated Models
item.description: arXiv:2604.21998v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Experimental designs that are minimax in the presence of model misspecifications have been constructed so as to minimize the maximum, over classes of alternate response models, of the integrated mean squared error of the predicted values. The theory to date has focussed almost exclusively on Least Squares estimates. Here we extend this theory to designs tailored for M-estimation of parameters, thus obtaining additional robustness against outlying, or otherwise erroneous, responses. We show that, subject to a minor change in a tuning constant, designs optimal for Least Squares remain so asymptotically for M-estimation, under squared error loss. We argue that even this minor change should be ignored, and the tuning constant chosen in an ad hoc but sensible manner that does not depend on which M-estimate is being employed. A rather surprising additional result is that our designs and estimates, derived under an assumption of i.i.d. errors, are also robust, in a minimax sense, against broad classes of correlation structures. We also investigate designs under a more robust loss function, less influenced by outlying responses than squared error.
item.dc:creator: Rui Hu, Douglas P. Wiens

item.title: Wasserstein convergence rates for empirical measures of point processes
item.description: arXiv:2604.23928v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we establish upper and lower bounds on the convergence rate of empirical measures of point processes under the Wasserstein distance. To this end, we first introduce a new metric on the space of finite counting measures. Unlike many existing metrics in the literature, our proposed metric incorporates the spatial locations of unmatched points. Drawing on both this new metric and existing metrics from the literature, we identify a set of common structural properties and develop a general framework for Wasserstein distances between point-process distributions based on metrics satisfying these properties. We then use this framework to investigate the convergence rates of empirical measures, providing quantitative guarantees for approximating the distribution of the underlying point process, and further establish corresponding concentration inequalities. These theoretical results may provide ingredients for constructing oracle goodness-of-fit tests for a specified point-process distribution. We also apply our theory to the approximation of Campbell measures and discuss how the resulting bounds can help assess Wasserstein-based learning of generative point-process models.
item.dc:creator: Dongzhou Huang, Tianyi Jiang, Haonan Wang

item.title: Sharp minimax risks and phase transitions in sparse submatrix detection
item.description: arXiv:2605.31583v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study the minimax risk of detecting a sparse, elevated-mean Gaussian submatrix planted in a larger noisy matrix. When the planted submatrix has size $n\times n$ and the ambient matrix has size $N\times N$ with $N=n^{1+\alpha}$, the seminal work of Butucea and Ingster (2013) identifies the sharp detection boundary around which the risk converges to $0$ or $1$. We extend that zero-one theory by determining sharp risk asymptotics throughout a two-parameter phase diagram. Above the boundary, the risk decays stretched- or super-exponentially fast, and we determine its precise exponent. Below the boundary, where the risk tends to $1$, we obtain matching absolute-constant bounds for its polynomial rate of convergence. In both regimes, the asymptotics change across the line $\alpha+\delta=1/2$, where $\delta$ parametrizes the signed distance from the detection boundary. Finally, on the boundary, we show that the minimax risk converges to the nondegenerate constant $\frac12$ in a very sparse regime where $n$ remains fixed and $N\to\infty$. Each of these rates corresponds to the risk of a suitably calibrated scan or sum test, whence follow the upper bounds. The main problem is to derive the matching regime-specific lower bounds. The mixture likelihood ratio is an average rather than a product and thus its logarithm lacks the additive structure required by standard large deviation formulations. On the other hand, classical second-moment estimates fail to be sharp due to overlap-induced correlations. To address these issues, we develop two general lower-bound principles based on truncated mixture likelihoods, tailored to the target risks on both sides of the detection boundary. The same framework yields sharp risk asymptotics for sparse subtensors with equal side lengths and also applies to more general testing problems including the detection of rectangular subtensors.
item.dc:creator: Subhajit Goswami, Rajarshi Mukherjee

item.title: Asymptotic Bayes Optimality Under Sparsity of the Gavrilov-Benjamini-Sarkar Step-Down Testing Procedure
item.description: arXiv:2607.03719v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this article, we investigate the asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity (ABOS) of the Gavrilov-Benjamini-Sarkar (GBS) step-down multiple testing procedure (Gavrilov et al., 2009) in the sparse Gaussian sequence model. While the asymptotic optimality properties of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure have been extensively studied, corresponding results for the GBS procedure remain unavailable despite its favorable finite-sample performance in several settings. Within the spike-and-slab Bayesian formulation and the asymptotic decision-theoretic framework of Bogdan et al. (2011), we establish that the GBS procedure is ABOS over a broad class of sparse asymptotic regimes. Existing analyses of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure rely on approximating the random rejection threshold by a suitable deterministic surrogate. In contrast, our approach proceeds through a direct analysis of the Bayes risk by separately controlling the false discovery and false nondiscovery components. The analysis combines two key ingredients: a new finite-sample inequality for shifted order statistics associated with the GBS critical constants and a signal-crossing argument for ordered alternative $p$-values that exploits the sequential step-down structure of the procedure. For diverging expected signal counts, these tools yield ABOS without threshold localization. For bounded positive expected signal counts, a direct argument based on the first GBS critical constant establishes ABOS as well. In particular, our results cover polynomial sparsity $p_m\asymp m^{-\beta}$ for every fixed $0<\beta\le1$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first asymptotic decision-theoretic analysis of the GBS procedure and the first proof of its asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity.
item.dc:creator: Prasenjit Ghosh, Arijit Chakrabarti

item.title: Sharp Asymptotic Minimaxity of the Gavrilov-Benjamini-Sarkar Step-Down Testing Procedure in Sparse Gaussian Sequence Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.05893v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: False discovery rate control does not by itself guarantee optimal recovery of sparse signals: a procedure may make few false discoveries while missing an unnecessarily large fraction of the alternatives. We investigate whether the classical Gavrilov--Benjamini--Sarkar (GBS) step-down procedure also achieves the sharp frequentist minimax limits for sparse recovery in independent Gaussian sequence models. Under a beta-min separation at the critical sparse detection boundary, GBS attains the exact asymptotic risk constant $\bar\Phi(b)$ for normalized Hamming loss and combined $\mathrm{FDP}+\mathrm{FNP}$ loss. The Hamming conclusion remains valid when the number of signals is only bounded above by the nominal sparsity $s_n$. For heterogeneous signal magnitudes, the corresponding risk under either loss equals the sharp benchmark $\Lambda_n(a)+o(1)$, without assuming that $\Lambda_n(a)$ converges; this is additive, rather than necessarily relative, sharpness. We assume $s_n\to\infty$, $n/s_n\to\infty$, and a vanishing nominal level $\alpha_n$ satisfying $\log(1/\alpha_n)=o(\sqrt{\log(n/s_n)})$. Unlike step-up rules, a step-down procedure must satisfy every preceding ordered $p$-value constraint before reaching a given rank. Our analysis handles this sequential obstruction directly: a finite-sample shifted order-statistic bound makes false positives negligible, while new uniform crossing arguments show that the rejection path reaches the optimal fraction of signals. The results extend the range of testing architectures known to attain the sharp minimax benchmarks, without requiring localization of a single rejection threshold.
item.dc:creator: Prasenjit Ghosh

item.title: The Randomized BH Procedure: A Generalized Framework Encompassing Conformal and Competition Tests
item.description: arXiv:2607.07245v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose the Randomized BH procedure, a generalized framework that introduces randomization into the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure for false discovery rate (FDR) control. We show that the classical BH procedure as well as two recently developed families of null-distribution-free methods, competition tests and conformal tests, share a common theoretical foundation and arise as special cases of this framework. The Randomized BH relaxes the classical conditions required for FDR control, frees conformal tests from the strict exchangeability assumption while allowing calibration sets to be constructed via pre-screening, and enables competition tests to be analyzed through the well-developed theory of p-values. We illustrate the framework through two applications. The first is a deeper analysis of compound p-values through the lens of randomization. The second is a general approach for integrating distributed multiple testing problems while maintaining global FDR control. Numerical simulations confirm the validity of our theoretical results.
item.dc:creator: Mingzhou Deng, Yan Fu

item.title: Exchangeable Testing Against an Unknown Benchmark
item.description: arXiv:2608.04838v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We generate infinite binary exchangeable sequences by sequential comparison of data points against a latent benchmark. Assuming a prior distribution of the benchmark rank \(R_0\) within an unobserved group of players, we set up the Bayesian machinery which determines the posterior distribution of the running rank \(R_n\) in purely combinatorial terms, by counting insertion slots in a uniformly random ranking. This yields an explicit predictive probability of winning against the benchmark, which is a rational function of the counts. We identify some cases where the predictive probability has particularly simple form, notably a tournament related to the Topp--Leone distribution. The running benchmark rank is a P\'olya urn with random initial composition, and its normalised value converges to a latent strength variable with polynomial density. In a projective time scale, the fluctuations of the normalised rank about this limit are Brownian, with the Wright--Fisher coefficient frozen at the limit, while the associated recurrent up-down Markov chain on a high level $n$ of the Pascal graph is approximated by a Wright--Fisher diffusion with a nonlinear drift expressed through the prior density.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Gnedin

item.title: Ultra-high-dimensional spot support screening in continuous-time regression
item.description: arXiv:2608.08582v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study variable screening for high-frequency continuous-time regression, targeting the support of the spot regression coefficient. Under coordinatewise truncation and finite-variation jumps, uniform entrywise bounds for local correlation estimates yield the rate $\{(\log p)/n\}^{\alpha/(2\alpha+1)}$ under a local averaged $\alpha$-H\"older condition, up to confidence and grid factors. These bounds imply sure screening for the marginal support. To retain the regression support under local dependence, we propose partial-residual spot iterative screening with pathwise Lepski adaptation. Under sparse eigenvalues and standardized beta-min, the procedure has the sure screening property and requires only correlation columns associated with the current active set. A list-size minimax lower bound applies to both support targets and matches the localization and multiplicity order of the marginal-screening bound when $\log(p/d)\asymp\log p$. Simulations and a high-frequency factor application illustrate the procedures.
item.dc:creator: Haibin Zhu

item.title: Improving the James-Stein estimator via q-number shrinkage
item.description: arXiv:2609.39614v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For estimating the mean vector of a $p$-variate normal distribution ($p \ge 3$) under quadratic loss, the positive-part James-Stein estimator dominates the original Jame-Stein estimator though it suffers from a non-smooth thresholding boundary. In this paper, we first express the shrinkage factor of the positive-part estimator using an infinite series. Truncating this series at a finite degree $m$ allows us to interpret the factor as a special case of $q$-numbers. Leveraging these $q$-numbers parameterized by a positive real index $m$, we propose a novel smooth estimator. We prove that the proposed estimator dominates the original James-Stein estimator for any dimension $p \ge 3$, provided the truncation parameter satisfies $m \ge 0.95\sqrt{p-2}$.
item.dc:creator: Yuzo Maruyama, Akimichi Takemura

item.title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Expected-Time Characterization
item.description: arXiv:2610.25821v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach spreads the initial wealth over fixed bets according to a prior distribution, using a universal portfolio algorithm. For suitable priors, this approach achieves the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, priors with this guarantee can behave quite differently near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and, under technical conditions, prove a sharp formula for expected rejection time, uniform over all bounded alternatives as the error probability tends to zero. The formula shows how the prior's mass around the zero bet determines the cost of adapting to an unknown alternative. We characterize the priors that attain the best possible leading constant when the error probability and alternative vary together. We also show that no valid test can uniformly improve on this cost across ranges of alternatives near the null. In particular, the uniform prior can require arbitrarily more observations than suitable priors that concentrate around the zero bet. A general inversion argument converts our results into sharp expected times to reach a prescribed confidence-sequence width. We also give a concrete prior choice and an FFT-based algorithm with almost linear computational complexity.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Orabona

item.title: Sharp Generalization for Nonparametric Regression in Interpolation Space by Over-Parameterized Neural Networks Trained with Preconditioned Gradient Descent and Early Stopping
item.description: arXiv:2407.11353v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study nonparametric regression using an over-parameterized two-layer neural network trained with algorithmic guarantees in this paper. We consider the setting where the training features are drawn uniformly from the unit sphere in $\RR^d$, and the target function lies in an interpolation space commonly studied in statistical learning theory. We demonstrate that training the neural network with a novel Preconditioned Gradient Descent (PGD) algorithm, equipped with early stopping, achieves a sharp regression rate of $\cO(n^{-\frac{2\alpha s'}{2\alpha s'+1}})$, where $\alpha$ parametrizes the polynomial eigenvalue decay of the regular Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), $\lambda_j\asymp j^{-2\alpha}$, and $2\alpha=d/(d-1)$ under the spherical uniform design considered here. The target function is assumed to belong to the interpolation space $\bth{\cH_K}^{s'}$ with $s'\ge3$. This rate is even sharper than the currently known nearly-optimal rate of $\cO(n^{-\frac{2\alpha s'}{2\alpha s'+1}})\log^2(1/\delta)$~\citep{Li2024-edr-general-domain}, where $n$ is the size of the training data and $\delta \in (0,1)$ is a small probability. Our analysis is based on two key technical contributions. First, we present a principled decomposition of the network output at each PGD step into a function in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of a newly induced integral kernel, and a residual function with small $L^{\infty}$-norm. Second, leveraging this decomposition, we apply local Rademacher complexity theory to tightly control the complexity of the function class comprising all the neural network functions obtained in the PGD iterates. Our results show how PGD changes the effective kernel in the reference training dynamics, inducing an integral kernel with lower complexity than the regular NTK arising from vanilla GD.
item.dc:creator: Yingzhen Yang, Ping Li

item.title: Diagonally-Weighted Generalized Method of Moments Estimation for Gaussian Mixture Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2507.20459v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With direct computation of moments through order $L$ in $d$ dimensions, standard method of moments (MM) incurs $\Omega(d^L)$ computation and storage costs, and standard generalized method of moments (GMM) additionally requires estimating and inverting an often ill-conditioned covariance matrix of size $\Omega(d^L)$-by-$\Omega(d^L)$ to obtain the optimal weighting matrix. Pereira, Kileel, and Kolda [arXiv:2202.06930 (2022)] avoid the tensor computation cost of MM through implicit moment computation. Despite this progress, incorporating statistically principled weighting while preserving computational efficiency remains an important challenge, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where sampling variances can differ substantially across moment orders. We introduce diagonally-weighted GMM (DGMM), which assigns one adaptive weight to each moment order through a structured approximation of the optimal weighting matrix while avoiding the covariance inversion, thereby balancing statistical efficiency, computational complexity, and numerical stability. For general parametric models, we prove that DGMM is consistent, asymptotically normal, and near-efficient under explicit structural conditions. For heteroscedastic low-rank Gaussian mixtures, we design a computationally efficient and numerically stable algorithm that extends the implicit moment computation to the DGMM objective, gradients, and weights and incorporates Nystr\"om approximations of the kernel sums. In low-SNR experiments with $d=100$ and $L=4$, where standard MM and GMM are infeasible, controlled weighting comparisons show that DGMM achieves consistently small parameter errors across tested initializations, including the challenging starts where alternative weightings struggle, with shorter median runtimes and fewer iterations. The code and data will be available upon publication at https://github.com/liu-lzhang/dgmm.
item.dc:creator: Liu Zhang, Oscar Mickelin, Sheng Xu, Amit Singer

item.title: Group Competition Test: A P-value-free False Discovery Rate Control Framework for Grouped Hypotheses
item.description: arXiv:2512.00901v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Grouped multiple testing arises in many high-dimensional applications, where hypotheses may differ across groups and valid p-values are unavailable. Applying competition-based procedures separately within groups can inflate the global false discovery rate (FDR), while conservative corrections may substantially reduce power. We extend the competition test framework to the grouped setting and propose two procedures. The group competition (GC) test provides finite-sample FDR bounds under arbitrary inter-group dependence. For homogeneous groups, the required correction has logarithmic order in the number of groups, and this order is unavoidable for the GC test. The consistent group competition (CGC) filter instead couples group-specific thresholds through a single global normalization. Under the stated basic-independence conditions, it controls the FDR in finite samples without a correction that grows with the number of groups; under arbitrary inter-group dependence, the same guarantee is retained with a per-group correction that depends on the symmetry parameter of each group. We further develop a parameterized-threshold analysis to establish asymptotic guarantees and to characterize when the per-group correction can be dropped, so that a simple filter still controls the FDR approximately. Simulation studies show that the GC test and the CGC filter can improve power over pooled competition testing in heterogeneous settings, whereas the pooled test may remain more powerful under homogeneity. A peptide-spectrum matching benchmark involving post-translational modifications illustrates the practical relevance of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Mingzhou Deng, Yan Fu

item.title: Decomposition of Spillover Effects Under Misspecification: Pseudo-true Estimands and a Local-Global Extension
item.description: arXiv:2602.12023v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To measure spillovers, researchers often summarize who else was treated with a simple measure, such as the share of treated neighbors. We study what the researcher estimates when that summary is misspecified. We show that the researcher estimates the best approximation to the true policy effect among all functionals of the chosen summary, and that the usual direct and spillover estimates are exactly the components of this approximation. We then specialize this framework to a setting common in applications such as cash transfers: treatment spills over both globally, through market equilibrium, and locally, through network externalities, while the researcher models only one channel. The network estimator still recovers the network spillover, and the equilibrium estimator the equilibrium spillover, even when the other channel is ignored. We illustrate with a simulation calibrated to a large cash-transfer experiment.
item.dc:creator: Yechan Park, Xiaodong Yang

item.title: Discussion on "Principled type I error rate inflation in two-arm clinical trial designs with external control information borrowing" by Silvia Calderazzo, Manuel Wiesenfarth, Vivienn Weru, and Annette Kopp-Schneider
item.description: arXiv:2610.00711v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Consideration of frequentist type-I error or power based on certain fixed conditions may not fully embrace the aims of a Bayesian analysis; this is particularly true in settings where informative priors are involved. Calderazzo et al. consider adaptations of a testing procedure involving Bayesian borrowing from external control data. Particular caution may be necessary here in order not to condition on parameters and data simultaneously. We consider their example case and argue that (a) the conditioning scheme may have limited practical implications, and (b) if the main concern are assumption violations, these might be better addressed by adapting the likelihood function.
item.dc:creator: Tim Friede, Christian R\"over
